26.text: Chapter Two: The reliability of those books, and the differences among them

Know that most of the books on which we have relied in transmission are well known and of established attribution to their authors — such as the books of al-Saduq, God have mercy on him, for apart from al-Hidaya, Sifat al-Shi'a, Fada'il al-Shi'a, Musadaqat al-Ikhwan and Fada'il al-Ashhur, they fall no way short in fame of the four books upon which everything turns in these times. They are included in our authorisations, and those eminent and excellent scholars who came after al-Saduq transmitted from them. The Book of al-Hidaya is also well known, though not to that degree (1). God has made available to us old and corrected copies of these: as for the Book of al-Amali, we found of it a corrected and vowelled copy written close to the age of the author, which had been read before many of the shaykhs and bore their authorisations. So too the Book of al-Khisal, which we collated against two old copies, one of which bore the authorisation of al-Shaykh Miqdad. So too the Book of Ikmal al-Din, which we had copied from an old book whose date of writing was close to the time of composition. And so too the Book of 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, peace be upon him, for we corrected its first part from a corrected copy said to be in the hand of its compiler, God have mercy on him — though in my view it was not in his hand, but bore his writing and his correction.

As for the Book of al-Imama, its author is among the greatest of the traditionists and jurists, and our scholars count his legal opinions among the reports themselves. An old, corrected copy of it reached us. The other primary work contains noble and solid reports with reliable chains, and the eminence of its author is apparent from it. The Book of Qurb al-Isnad is among the reliable and well-known primary works; we copied it from an old copy taken from the hand of al-Shaykh Muhammad b. Idris, upon which was the following in his own hand: "The original

In one copy: "And as for the Book of Da'a'im al-Islam which we have, I consider it possible that it is the composition of some other of the leading scholars." (It has already been stated that it is by the judge al-Nu'man b. Muhammad.)

27.text: from which I transmitted it contained plain solecisms and disordered wording, so I have reproduced it as I found it, for fear of altering and changing it. Let whoever looks into it find an excuse for me, for I have set out my excuse in the matter."
The Book of Basa'ir al-Darajat is among the reliable primary works from which al-Kulayni and others transmitted.

The books of al-Shaykh are likewise among the well-known books, except the Book of al-Amali, which is not as widely known as the rest of his books; yet we found old copies of it bearing the authorisations of eminent scholars, and we found what the traditionists and scholars after him transmitted from it to agree with what is in it.

The Amali of his learned son is, in our time, better known than his own Amali, and most people suppose it to be al-Shaykh's Amali — which is not so, as has become clear to me from evident indications. Yet his son's Amali falls no way short of his own in reliability and renown, even if al-Shaykh's Amali is, in my view, sounder and more trustworthy.

The Book of al-Irshad is better known than its author, God have mercy on him. Of the Book of al-Majalis we found old copies, and the indications point to its soundness (1). As for the Book of al-Ikhtisas, it is an elegant book containing the circumstances of the companions of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family, and of the Imams, peace be upon them, and in it are rare reports. I transmitted it from an old copy, upon whose title was written: "A book extracted from the Book of al-Ikhtisas, the composition of Abu 'Ali Ahmad b. al-Husayn b. Ahmad b. 'Imran, God have mercy on him." Yet after the preface it ran thus: "Muhammad b. Muhammad b. al-Nu'man said: There narrated to me Abu Ghalib Ahmad b. Muhammad al-Zurari and Ja'far b. Muhammad b. Qulawayh…" to the end of the chain; and so to the end of the book it begins from the shaykhs of al-Shaykh al-Mufid. So it appears that it is among the compositions of al-Mufid, God have mercy on him. The rest of his books are too well known to need comment.
The Book of Kamil al-Ziyara is among the recognised primary works; al-Shaykh drew upon it in al-Tahdhib, as did other traditionists.
The Book of al-Mahasin of al-Barqi is among the reliable primary works; al-Kulayni transmitted from it, as did every compiler after him.
The commentary of 'Ali b. Ibrahim is among the recognised books; al-Tabrisi and others transmitted from it.
In one copy: "And the Book of al-Nusus is likewise only presumed to be his, though it may be by one of the eminent scholars of his age; it is sometimes ascribed to Muhammad b. 'Ali al-Qummi."

28.text: As for the Book of al-'Ilal, although its author is not mentioned in the books of rijal, its reports are carefully set down and agree with what his father, al-Saduq and others transmitted; and its author is mentioned in the chains of certain narrations. Al-Kulayni transmitted, in the chapter on those who saw the Qa'im, peace be upon him, from Muhammad and al-Hasan, the two sons of 'Ali b. Ibrahim, through the intermediacy of 'Ali b. Muhammad; and likewise in another place in that chapter from him alone through the same intermediary. This is among what supports relying upon him, though it is not free of oddity, since he transmits a great deal from 'Ali b. Ibrahim without an intermediary. Indeed the more evident view, as has lately occurred to me, is that he is Muhammad b. 'Ali b. Ibrahim b. Muhammad al-Hamadani, who was the agent of the Sacred Precinct, as I have explained in my notes on al-Kafi.

As for the commentary of al-'Ayyashi, al-Tabrisi and others transmitted from it, and we have seen two old copies of it. It is counted among his books in the works of rijal; but one of the copyists deleted its chains for the sake of brevity and offered at its beginning an excuse more objectionable than his offence.

The commentary of the Imam, peace be upon him, is among the recognised books. Al-Saduq relied upon it and drew from it, even though some traditionists have impugned it; yet al-Saduq, God have mercy on him, was better informed and closer in time than those who impugned it, and most scholars have transmitted from it without casting doubt upon it.

As for the Book of Rawdat al-Wa'izin, we have already stated that it is included in the authorisations of the leading scholars and that eminent and noble men transmitted from it; and you have learned its condition and that of its author from what we quoted from our illustrious predecessors. So too the Book of I'lam al-Wara, whose author is too well known to need comment; my copy is in the hand of its author, God have mercy on him.
The Epistle on Etiquette is likewise recognised; his son drew upon it in al-Makarim. As for his two commentaries, the large and the small, they need no advertising.
The Book of al-Makarim is, in its fame, like the sun at midday, and a number of excellent scholars have praised its author.
The Book of Mishkat al-Anwar is a fine book containing rare reports.

As for the Book of al-Ihtijaj, although most of its reports lack complete chains, it is among the recognised and widely circulated books. Al-Sayyid b. Tawus praised both the book and its author, and most of the later scholars have drawn upon it.

29.text: The two books al-Manaqib and al-Ma'alim are among the reliable books; the authors of the authorisations mentioned them, and their author is too well known in learning, trustworthiness and eminence for his condition to be hidden from anyone.
Bayan al-Tanzil is a small book of many benefits; we have taken only a little from it, since most of it is set down elsewhere.
The Book of Kashf al-Ghumma is among the best known of books, and its author is among the Imami scholars named in the chains of the authorisations.

Of the Book of Tuhaf al-'Uqul we came upon an old copy; its arrangement points to the loftiness of its author's standing. Most of it consists of admonitions and of well-established principles for which we need no chain.

The Book of al-'Umda and its author are both well known and named in the chains of the authorisations, and so likewise al-Manaqib. As for al-Mustadrak, we have an old copy of it which we suppose to be in the hand of its author. The Book of al-Kifaya is a noble book; nothing like it has been composed on the Imamate. This book and its author are named in the authorisation of al-'Allama and elsewhere, and its composition is the clearest proof of his learning, trustworthiness and piety. Al-'Allama attested his trustworthiness in al-Khulasa, saying: "He was trustworthy, one of our companions, a jurist of standing." And Ibn Shahrashub said in al-Ma'alim: "'Ali b. Muhammad b. 'Ali al-Khazzaz al-Razi, also called al-Qummi; he has books on theology and on jurisprudence, among them al-Kifaya fi'l-Nusus." So too the Book of Tanbih al-Khatir and its author are named in the authorisations and well known; but since his book was confined to admonitions and maxims, he did not, God have mercy on him, sift the poor from the sound, and mixed the reports of the Imamiyya with the traditions of those who differ from us. For that reason we have not set down everything in that book, but have confined ourselves to transmitting what is more reliable — for by the blessings of the pure Imams, peace be upon them, we have no need of the reports of those who differ from us.
As for the two books Mashariq al-Anwar and al-Alfayn, you have learned their condition.

The compositions of al-Shahid are as well known as their learned author, except the Book of al-Istidrak, for I did not come upon the original of the book; I found reports taken from it in the hand of the eminent Shaykh Muhammad b. 'Ali al-Juba'i, who stated that he had transmitted them from the hand of al-Shahid, may God raise his rank. And al-Durra al-Bahira, which did not

30.text: become as widely known as the rest of his books; it is confined to setting down brief sayings handed down from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family, and from each of the Imams, God's blessings be upon them all.
The books of the two eminent Sayyids, like their authors, need no comment.

The Book of Tibb al-A'imma is among the well-known books, though it is not on the level of the rest, its author being unknown. That does no harm, since little of it bears upon the derivative rulings; and in matters of remedies and supplications we have no need of strong chains.

The Book of Sahifat al-Rida, peace be upon him, is among the books well known to both the Shi'a and the wider community. The eminent Sayyid 'Ali b. Tawus transmitted from it by his chain to al-Shaykh al-Tabrisi, God have mercy on him; and I found in the old copies of it chains to the said Shaykh and from him to the Imam, peace be upon him. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Book of Rabi' al-Abrar: "Yahya b. al-Husayn al-Husayni used to say of the chain of the Sahifat al-Rida: were this chain recited into the ear of a madman he would recover his senses." Al-Najashi referred to it in his notice on 'Abd Allah b. Ahmad b. 'Amir al-Ta'i and on his father, the transmitter of this epistle; he praised it and gave his chain to it. In sum, it is among the well-known primary works and may soundly be relied upon.

So too the Book of Tibb al-Rida, peace be upon him, is among the recognised books. Al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din mentioned in the Fihrist that al-Sayyid Fadl Allah b. 'Ali al-Rawandi wrote a commentary upon it which he named Tarjamat al-'Alawi li'l-Tibb al-Radawi. And Ibn Shahrashub said in al-Ma'alim, in his notice on Muhammad b. al-Hasan b. Jumhur al-Qummi: "He has al-Malahim wa'l-Fitan, al-Wahida, and the Golden Epistle from al-Rida, God's blessings be upon him, on medicine." End of quotation. Al-Shaykh mentioned the like of this in the Fihrist and gave his chain to it; we shall set it down in full in the Book of the Heavens and the World, in the chapters on medicine.
As for the Book of Fiqh al-Rida, peace be upon him, you have learned its condition.
The Book of al-Masa'il — its traditions agree with what is in the books in circulation, and its transmitter is too well known for his condition and eminence to be hidden from anyone.
The two books al-Khara'ij and Fiqh al-Qur'an are of established attribution to their author, who is among

31.text: the eminent and trustworthy of our companions; the two books are named in the catalogues of the scholars, and our companions have transmitted from them.

Of the Book of al-Du'a' we found an old copy; in it are brief and noble supplications taken from the reliable primary works — and in any case the matter of a chain in supplication is of little consequence.
As for the Book of al-Qisas, you have learned its condition; we collated it against a copy bearing the hand and the correction of al-Shahid al-Thani, God have mercy on him.
The Book of Daw' al-Shihab is a noble book containing abundant benefits absent from the books of both the Shi'a and the wider community.
The Book of al-Lubab contains some benefits.
The commentary on the Nahj is well known and recognised; most of the commentators have had recourse to it.
The Book of Asbab al-Nuzul contains benefits.

The books of the eminent Sayyids, the sons of Tawus, are all recognised. We have left aside among them the Book of Rabi' al-Shi'a, since it agrees with the Book of I'lam al-Wara in all its chapters and arrangement — which is a matter for wonder.
As for the Book of Ta'wil al-Ayat and the Book of Kanz Jami' al-Fawa'id, I have seen a number of later scholars transmit from them, and their author is of the utmost learning and piety.

The Book of Ghawali al-La'ali, although well known and its author recognised for learning, did not sift the husk from the kernel, and brought the reports of the bigots among those who differ from us in among the narrations of our companions; for that reason we have confined ourselves to transmitting only some of it. The like holds of the Book of Nathr al-La'ali and the Book of Jami' al-Akhbar.

The Book of al-Nu'mani is among the most eminent of books. Al-Shaykh al-Mufid, God have mercy on him, said in his Irshad, after setting down the explicit designations of the Imamate of the Proof — upon him and upon his forefathers be blessings and peace: "The narrations on this are many, and the traditionists of this party have recorded them in their books. Among those who established them with exposition and detail is Muhammad b. Ibrahim, with the agnomen Abu 'Abd Allah al-Nu'mani, in the book he composed on the Occultation."

32.text: The Book of al-Rawda does not stand at a high level of reliability.

As for the two books al-Tawhid and al-Ihlilaja, you have learned their condition, and their manner of expression points to their soundness. Ibn Shahrashub said in al-Ma'alim: "Al-Mufaddal b. 'Umar has a testament."

The Book of al-Ihlilaja is from the dictation of al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, on divine unity; and some of the scholars of those who differ from us have likewise ascribed this book to him, peace be upon him. Al-Najashi said in his notice on al-Mufaddal: "He has a Book of Reflection" — a book on the beginning of creation and on urging men to draw lessons; perhaps this is a reference to al-Tawhid. And he counted the Book of al-Ihlilaja among the books of Hamdan b. al-Mu'afa; perhaps the meaning is that it is among what he transmitted.

As for the Book of Misbah al-Shari'a, it contains some matter that gives the discerning and skilled reader pause, and its manner does not resemble the rest of the sayings and traditions of the Imams. Al-Shaykh transmitted some of its reports in his Majalis thus: "There informed us a company, from Abu al-Mufaddal al-Shaybani, by his chain from Shaqiq al-Balkhi, from one of the people of learning who informed him." This indicates that the book was with al-Shaykh, God have mercy on him, and existed in his time, and that he drew from it — yet without placing complete trust in it, nor was it established with him that it was transmitted from al-Sadiq, peace be upon him. Its chain terminates among the Sufis, and for that reason it takes in many of their technical terms and transmission from their shaykhs and from those upon whom they rely in their narrations. And God knows.

As for the two books of commentary, their two transmitters are reliable and well known, and their contents agree with one another and with the rest of the reports; 'Ali b. Ibrahim and other excellent scholars drew upon them. Al-Najashi counted among the books of Sa'd b. 'Abd Allah the Book of Nasikh al-Qur'an wa Mansukhihi wa Muhkamihi wa Mutashabihihi, and gave sound chains to his books.

The Book of al-Maqalat was counted by al-Shaykh and al-Najashi among the books of Sa'd, and both set down their sound chains to it. Its author is beyond description in trustworthiness, learning and eminence; al-Shaykh transmitted from this book in the Book of al-Ghayba, as did al-Kashshi in the Book of al-Rijal.

The Book of Sulaym b. Qays is of the utmost fame. A number of scholars have impugned it, but the truth is that it is among the reliable primary works; we shall discuss it and its like in the last volume of our book, and shall set down its chain in the fifth section.

33.text: As for the Book of Qabas al-Misbah, you have learned the eminence of its author, besides which it is confined to supplication.
The books of al-Bayadi and Ibn Sulayman are all fit to be relied upon; their two authors are among the stalwart scholars, and the utmost solidity and soundness is apparent in them.
As for the Book of al-Sara'ir, reliance upon it and upon its author is no secret to men of discernment.
The Book of Irshad al-Qulub is an elegant book containing solid and rare reports.

From the two books A'lam al-Din and Ghurar al-Akhbar we have transmitted few reports, since most of their reports are set down in books more reliable than they — even though the eminence of their author is apparent from the whole and from the transmission of the great scholars from them.

The ancient book is wholly on supplications. It contains complete, eloquent and rare supplications, from each of which the light of inimitability and of instruction shines forth; every clause of them is an upright witness to their issuing from the Imams of mankind and the princes of speech. Al-Sayyid b. Tawus, God have mercy on him, transmitted much from it in al-Muhaj and elsewhere. The date of writing of the copy from which we extracted was the year five hundred and seventy-six. It appears from al-Kaf'ami that it is the collection of supplications of the eminent Shaykh Abu al-Husayn Muhammad b. Harun al-Tal'ukbari, who is among the greatest of the traditionists.

The two books of rijal are what the excellent scholars turn upon in every age and land. From them we confine ourselves to setting down what concerns matters other than the establishing of the circumstances of transmitters — that is, what bears upon the other chapters.

The Book of Bisharat al-Mustafa is among the well-known books; many of our scholars have transmitted from it, and its author is among the most eminent traditionists. He occurs in most of our chains to the Shaykh of the community, and he transmits from Abu 'Ali, son of the Shaykh of the community, all his books and narrations. Al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din said in the Fihrist: "The Shaykh and Imam 'Imad al-Din Muhammad b. Abi al-Qasim al-Tabari, a trustworthy jurist; he studied under al-Shaykh Abu 'Ali al-Tusi and has compositions; Qutb al-Din al-Rawandi studied under him."

The eminence of al-Husayn b. Sa'id and of Ahmad b. Muhammad b. 'Isa spares us any need to treat of the condition of their compositions; and the attribution of the Book of al-Zuhd to al-Husayn is established.
As for the other primary work, its opening ran thus: "Ahmad b. Muhammad b. 'Isa, from al-Husayn b. Sa'id";

34.text: then in the remaining chapters it begins with the shaykhs of al-Husayn. This gives rise to the supposition that it is his; yet it may be by Ahmad, on account of certain indications, as we have noted, and because the book opens with him.

As for the Book of al-'Uyun wa'l-Mahasin, since it is confined to maxims and admonitions, our ignorance of its author does us no harm. We have of it an old, corrected copy. It contains the choice sayings, and adds to them many of the precious maxims which al-Amidi did not come upon. It appears from what we shall quote from Ibn Shahrashub that al-Amidi was among our scholars and that he authorised him to transmit this book. He said in Ma'alim al-'Ulama': "'Abd al-Wahid b. Muhammad b. 'Abd al-Wahid al-Amidi al-Tamimi; he has Ghurar al-Hikam wa Durar al-Kalim, in which he sets down the sayings and maxims of the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him."
The fame of al-Kaf'ami's books and the learning of their author spare us any need to treat of their condition or of his.
The Book of Qada' al-Huquq is a good book containing fine reports.

As for the books of al-Sayyid Baha' al-Din b. 'Abd al-Hamid: the first two contain rare reports on the return and on the circumstances of the Qa'im, peace be upon him; the third takes in the merits of the Imams, the manner of the martyrdom of the Master of Martyrs and of his blessed companions, peace be upon him and upon them, and an account of al-Mukhtar's rising to seek vengeance together with the sum of his circumstances; and the fourth contains rare reports. The said Sayyid is among the most eminent of the naqibs and the distinguished.

The solidity of the Book of al-Tamhis points to the learning of its author; and if its author is Abu 'Ali, as appears to be the case, then his learning and his attested trustworthiness are well known.
The books of the two eminent scholars al-'Allama and Ibn Fahd, God sanctify the spirits of them both, are in fame and reliability as their authors are.

The Book of al-'Adad is an elegant book on the deeds of the days of the months and their auspicious and inauspicious days; half of it has come into our hands. Its author is known for learning and named in the authorisations; he is the brother of al-'Allama al-Hilli, God sanctify their subtle spirits.
As for al-Shaykh Ibn Nama and al-Sayyid Fakhkhar, they are among the most eminent of our transmitters and shaykhs; mention of them will come in the authorisations of our companions.

35.text: The Book of al-Ghurar contains eminent reports together with their exposition, and its author is among the excellent Sayyids. He transmits from Ibn Shahrashub, from 'Ali b. Sa'id b. Hibat Allah al-Rawandi, from 'Abd Allah b. Ja'far al-Duristi, and from other eminent and leading scholars.

As for al-Mazar al-Kabir, the manner of its chains shows it to be a reliable book; the two Sayyids, the sons of Tawus, took many reports and visitations from it. Al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din said in the Fihrist: "Al-Sayyid Abu al-Barakat Muhammad b. Isma'il al-Mashhadi, a trustworthy jurist and traditionist; he studied under the Imam Muhyi al-Din al-Husayn b. al-Muzaffar al-Hamadani." And in his notice on al-Hamadani he said: "Al-Sayyid Abu al-Barakat al-Mashhadi informed us of his books."

As for al-Karajaki, he is among the most eminent of scholars, jurists and theologians; all the holders of authorisations give their chains to him. His Book of Kanz al-Fawa'id is among the well-known books from which most who came after him drew, and the rest of his books are of the utmost solidity. Al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din said in his Fihrist: "The learned and trustworthy Shaykh Abu al-Fath Muhammad b. 'Ali al-Karajaki, the jurist of the companions; he studied under al-Sayyid al-Murtada 'Alam al-Huda and al-Shaykh al-Muwaffaq Abu Ja'far, God have mercy on them both. He has compositions, among them the Book of al-Ta'ajjub and the Book of al-Nawadir. Our father informed us, from his father, from him." End of quotation. It appears from the authorisations that he was the teacher of Ibn al-Barraj.

Al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din is among the well-known trustworthy men and traditionists, and his Fihrist is of the utmost fame. He is among the descendants of al-Husayn b. 'Ali b. Babawayh, and al-Saduq is his great-uncle. Al-Shahid al-Thani said in the Book of Authorisation: "And I have authorised him to transmit from me all that was transmitted by 'Ali b. 'Ubayd Allah b. al-Hasan b. al-Husayn b. al-Hasan b. al-Husayn b. 'Ali b. al-Husayn b. Babawayh, and all that his Fihrist contains of the names of the scholars later than al-Shaykh Abu Ja'far al-Tusi. This man was of good precision and transmitted a great deal from numerous shaykhs." End of quotation. His Arba'in contains rare and elegant reports.
The Book of al-Tuhfa is a book of many benefits, yet we have transmitted from it only rarely, since its reports are taken from books better known than it.

36.text: As for Ibn Shadhan, you have learned his condition.

As for al-Mas'udi, al-Najashi counted him in his Fihrist among the transmitters of the Shi'a and said: "He has books, among them the Book of Ithbat al-Wasiyya li-'Ali b. Abi Talib, peace be upon them both, and the Book of Muruj al-Dhahab. He died in the year three hundred and thirty-three."

As for the Book of al-Nawadir, its author is among the noble and eminent. Al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din said in the Fihrist: "The scholar of his age; he combined with loftiness of lineage the perfection of learning and standing, and was the teacher of the leading men of his time. He has compositions; I met him and read some of them before him." End of quotation. Most of the traditions of this book are taken from the books of Musa b. Isma'il b. Musa b. Ja'far, peace be upon them both, which Sahl b. Ahmad al-Dibaji transmitted from Muhammad b. Muhammad b. al-Ash'ath, from him. As for Sahl, al-Najashi praised him; and Ibn al-Ghada'iri, after censuring him, said: "There is no harm in what is transmitted of the Ash'athiyyat and the like of them, of what others have transmitted." As for Ibn al-Ash'ath, al-Najashi attested his trustworthiness and said that he transmits a recension from Musa b. Isma'il. Al-Saduq transmitted from his book in al-Majalis by another chain, thus: "There narrated to us al-Hasan b. Ahmad b. Idris, from his father, from Ahmad b. Muhammad b. 'Isa, from Muhammad b. Yahya al-Khazzaz, from Musa b. Isma'il." By these indications, acting upon its traditions is strengthened. As for Ad'iyat al-Sirr, we shall set them down in full in their place.

As for the Book of al-Fada'il and the Book of Izahat al-'Illa, their author is among the most eminent of the trustworthy and learned, and the holders of authorisations have praised him greatly. Al-Shahid, God sanctify his secret, said in al-Dhikra: "The Shaykh Abu al-Fadl Shadhan b. Jibra'il al-Qummi — who is among our eminent jurists — mentioned in the Book of Izahat al-'Illa fi Ma'rifat al-Qibla…", and then he set down a portion of it. As for the Book of Siffin, it is a reliable book from which al-Kulayni and the other traditionists drew. Al-Najashi said: "Nasr b. Muzahim al-Minqari al-'Attar, Abu al-Mufaddal, a Kufan of upright method and sound conduct, save that he transmits from the weak. His books are excellent, among them the Book of al-Jamal and the Book of Siffin." And he set down his chains to the two books and to the rest of his books; al-Shaykh likewise set down in the Fihrist his chain to his books.

37.text: As for the Book of al-Gharat, its author is among the well-known traditionists. Al-Najashi and al-Shaykh mentioned him, counted the Book of al-Gharat among his books and praised him, saying that he was a Zaydi and then became an Imami. Al-Sayyid b. Tawus transmitted many traditions from his books. One of the eminent traditionists informed us that he had found a sound, vowelled and old copy of it, written close to the time of the compiler and bearing the hands of a number of eminent scholars, and that he had it copied from that; so we took a copy from him. It agrees with what Ibn Abi al-Hadid and others extracted from it.

As for the Book of al-Muqtadab, al-Shaykh and al-Najashi mentioned it in their catalogues, counted this book among his books and praised him for the abundance of his transmission — yet they ascribed to him that he became confused at the end of his life. Ibn Shahrashub mentioned him and listed his compositions without impugning him in anything. In sum, his book is among the primary works reliable in the eyes of the Shi'a, as appears upon investigation.
The fame of al-Shahid al-Thani and of al-Muhaqqiq spares us any need to treat of the condition of their books; God illumine their tombs.
Al-Muhaqqiq al-Bahrani is among the most eminent and best known of scholars, and his two books are of the utmost fame.

As for the commentary of Furat: although our companions have treated its author with neither praise nor censure, the fact that its reports agree with the reliable traditions that have reached us, and the good precision of his transmission of them, is what yields confidence in its author and a good opinion of him. Al-Saduq, God have mercy on him, transmitted reports from him through the intermediacy of al-Hasan b. Muhammad b. Sa'id al-Hashimi; and al-Hakim Abu al-Qasim al-Haskani transmitted from him in Shawahid al-Tanzil and elsewhere.

As for the four books of Ja'far b. Ahmad, some are on the merits and some on character, etiquette and rulings; the legal rulings in them are rare. Their author is not mentioned in the books of rijal, but he is among the early scholars, close to the age of al-Mufid or in his age. He transmits from al-Safwani, the transmitter of al-Kulayni, through an intermediary, and also transmits from al-Saduq, as will come in the chain of the commentary of the Imam, peace be upon him. In them are fine and rare reports, and we have old corrected copies of them. Al-Sayyid b. Tawus transmits from his books in the Book of al-Iqbal and elsewhere, which supports reliance upon them. Al-Shahid al-Thani, God have mercy on him, transmitted from some of his books in

38.text: the Commentary on al-Irshad, on the merit of the congregational prayer, as did other eminent scholars.

As for the Book of Nuzhat al-Nazir and al-Jami', their author is among the well-known and exacting scholars; his opinions circulate among the later scholars, and he is the paternal cousin of al-Muhaqqiq, the author of al-Shara'i' and al-Mu'tabar.

The Book of al-Wasila and its author are both well known, and his opinions circulate among the later scholars. Al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din said: "The Shaykh and Imam 'Imad al-Din Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. 'Ali b. Hamza al-Tusi al-Mashhadi, a learned jurist and preacher; he has compositions, among them al-Wasila."

As for the books of the noble shaykhs and illustrious masters al-Shaykh Hasan, al-Sayyid Muhammad and al-Shaykh al-Baha'i — God illumine their resting places — their eminence and the distinction of their authors are well known; and so too the two books of our master Muhammad Amin, God sanctify his secret.
Al-Sayyid b. Baqi is of the utmost learning and accomplishment, though most of his book is taken from the Misbah of al-Shaykh, God have mercy on him.
The Book of Taqrib al-Ma'arif is a good book on theology containing fine reports, some of which we have set down in the Book of Trials; and the standing of its author is too great to need comment.
So too the books of the two eminent Shaykhs Ibn al-Barraj and Sallar are, like their authors, of the utmost reliability.

As for the Book of Da'a'im al-Islam, most of the people of our age used to imagine that it was the composition of al-Saduq, God have mercy on him. It has become clear to us that it is the composition of Abu Hanifa al-Nu'man b. Muhammad b. Mansur, judge of Egypt in the days of the Isma'ili dynasty. He was at first a Maliki, then was guided aright and became an Imami. Most of the reports of this book agree with what is in our well-known books, save that he did not transmit from the Imams after al-Sadiq, out of fear of the Isma'ili caliphs; yet beneath the veil of dissimulation he disclosed the truth to whoever looks into it deeply. His reports are fit to serve for corroboration and confirmation. Ibn Khallikan said: "He is one of the eminent men who are looked to. The Amir al-Mukhtar al-Masihi mentioned him in his history and said: he was of such learning, jurisprudence, religion and distinction as could not be surpassed. He has several compositions, among them the Book of Ikhtilaf Usul al-Madhahib and others." End of quotation. He was of the Maliki school and then passed over to the school of the Imamiyya. Ibn Zulaq said in his notice on his son 'Ali b. al-Nu'man: "His father al-Nu'man b. Muhammad the judge was of the utmost learning, one of the people of

39.text: the Qur'an and knowledge of its meanings, learned in the aspects of jurisprudence, in the science of the disagreements of the jurists, in lexicography, in poetry, and in acquaintance with the days of men, together with intelligence and fairness. He composed for the People of the House thousands of pages of books, in the finest composition and the most agreeable rhymed prose, and produced on the merits and the faults an excellent book. He has refutations of his opponents: a refutation of Abu Hanifa, of Malik, of al-Shafi'i and of Ibn Shurayh; and a Book of Disagreement in which he champions the People of the House, peace be upon them." I say: he then set down much of his merits and circumstances, and al-Yafi'i and others mentioned the like. Ibn Shahrashub said in the Book of Ma'alim al-'Ulama': "The judge al-Nu'man b. Muhammad is not an Imami, and his books are excellent; among them Sharh al-Akhbar fi Fada'il al-A'imma al-Athar, in which he sets down the merits down to al-Sadiq, peace be upon him; al-Ittifaq wa'l-Iftiraq; al-Manaqib wa'l-Mathalib; al-Imama; Usul al-Madhahib; al-Dawla; al-Idah." End of quotation.
The Book of al-Manaqib wa'l-Mathalib is an elegant book containing eminent benefits.
The book of al-Husayn b. Hamdan contains many reports on the merits, though some of the scholars of rijal have cast doubt upon him.

As for Ibn al-Khashshab, his history is well known; the author of Kashf al-Ghumma drew from it, and its reports are reliable. It is a small book confined to their births and deaths and the spans of their lives, peace be upon them.

The Book of al-Burhan is a solid book containing rare reports, and its author is among the well-known eminent scholars. Al-Najashi said: "'Ali b. Muhammad al-'Adawi al-Shimshati was a shaykh in al-Jazira, the most learned and most cultivated man of his time." He then listed many compositions of his and counted this book among them.

The epistle of Abu Ghalib contains the circumstances of Zurara b. A'yan, his brothers, their children and grandchildren, their chains, their books and their narrations; in it are abundant benefits. This man — I mean Ahmad b. Muhammad b. Sulayman b. al-Hasan b. al-Jahm b. Bukayr b. A'yan b. Sinsin, titled Abu Ghalib al-Zurari — was among the most eminent of the trustworthy and of the traditionists, and was teacher of the leading eminent scholars such as al-Shaykh al-Mufid, Ibn al-Ghada'iri and Ibn 'Abdun, God sanctify their secrets. Al-Najashi and others counted this epistle among his books, and we shall set the epistle down in full in the last of the volumes of this book, if God the Exalted wills.
The Book of Dala'il al-Imama is among the reliable and well-known books; most who came after him drew from it,

40.text: such as al-Sayyid b. Tawus and others. We found an old, corrected copy of it in the library of our master the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him. Its author is among the trustworthy transmitters of our Imami community, and he is not Ibn Jarir the historian, who differs from us. Al-Najashi, God have mercy on him, said: "Muhammad b. Jarir b. Rustam al-Tabari al-Amuli, Abu Ja'far, an eminent man among our companions, of much learning and excellent theology, trustworthy in hadith. He has the Book of al-Mustarshid fi Dala'il al-Imama. There informed us Ahmad b. 'Ali b. Nuh, from al-Hasan b. Hamza al-Tabari, who said: There narrated to us Muhammad b. Jarir b. Rustam this book and the rest of his books." And al-Shaykh said in the Fihrist: "Muhammad b. Jarir b. Rustam al-Tabari the elder, with the agnomen Abu Ja'far, religious and learned; he is not the author of the History, for that man was of the wider community's school. He has numerous books, among them the Book of al-Mustarshid."

The Book of Misbah al-Anwar contains choice reports, and it appears from the book that its author is among the great eminent scholars; he transmits from the reliable primary works of both the Shi'a and the wider community.

The Book of al-Durr al-Nazim is a noble and generous book containing many reports on the merits, by our paths and by the paths of those who differ from us. It sometimes transmits from the Book of Madinat al-'Ilm and from other reliable books. Its author was a contemporary of al-Sayyid 'Ali b. Tawus, God have mercy on him; we have seldom had recourse to it, for certain reasons.
As for the Book of al-Arba'in, most of our scholars have drawn from it and relied upon it.
The Book of Tasliyat al-Majalis — its author is among the eminent Sayyids of the later scholars. It is a large book containing many reports, some of which we have set down in the tenth volume.
The Book of Safwat al-Akhbar and Riyad al-Jinan contain rare reports on the merits; we have extracted from them what agrees with the reports of the reliable books.
As for the Book of al-Ghunya, its author has no need of praise; he is among the most eminent jurists, and his books are reliable and well known, this book above all.
The books of al-Muhaqqiq al-Tusi — God rest his sanctified spirit — and their author are better known than the sun at midday.

Al-Sayyid 'Amid al-Din is among the well-known scholars; the holders of authorisations have praised him, and his books are recognised and in circulation, though we have had recourse to them only a little.

41.text: So too the most eminent Shaykh al-Miqdad b. 'Abd Allah is among the most eminent jurists, and his compositions are of the utmost reliability and fame.
So too Fakhr al-Muhaqqiqin, the most exacting of the later jurists; his books are in circulation and recognised.
The Book of al-Adwa' contains many benefits, though we have not had recourse to it often.

As for the Shaykh who promoted the school, Nur al-Din — may God gather him with the pure Imams — his claims upon the faith and its people are greater than the least of them could be thanked for, and his compositions are of the utmost gravity and solidity.

And the guided martyr al-Sayyid al-Tustari — may God gather him with the first of the martyrs — expended every effort in aiding the manifest religion and repelling the doubts of those who differ from us. His books are recognised, though we have taken their reports from their own sources.
Al-Shaykh Ibn Dawud is of the utmost fame among the later scholars, and they have gone to lengths in praising him in the authorisations; our recourse to his books has been slight.

So too the Rijal of Ibn al-Ghada'iri: if its author is al-Husayn, then he is among the most eminent of the trustworthy; but if he is Ahmad, as appears to be the case, then I do not rely upon him greatly. In any case, relying upon this book would require rejecting most of the reports of the well-known books.
The two books of al-Malhama are well known, but I do not rely upon them greatly.

As for the Book of al-Anwar, some of the companions of al-Shahid al-Thani praised its author and counted him among his shaykhs. The contents of its reports agree with the reliable reports transmitted by sound chains, and it was well known among our scholars, who used to recite it in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal in gatherings and assemblies until the day of the noble birth. So too the other two books are reliable, and we have set down some of their reports in this book.

The book of Ahmad b. Abi Tahir contains the sermon of Fatima, God's blessings be upon her, and the sermons of the women of the People of the House, peace be upon them, at Karbala; its author is reliable in the eyes of both parties.

And the most glorious Sayyid Mirza Muhammad, God sanctify his spirit, was among the distinguished and eminent and among the godfearing and exemplary. He dwelt near the Sacred House of God until he passed to God's mercy, and his books are of the utmost solidity and soundness.

42.text: As for the Book of the Diwan, its attribution to him, God's blessings be upon him, is well known, and many of the verses set down in it are transmitted in other books; yet it is difficult to judge the whole of it sound. From the Ma'alim of Ibn Shahrashub it may be gathered that it is the composition of 'Ali b. Ahmad al-Adib al-Naysaburi, one of our scholars; and al-Najashi counted among the books of 'Abd al-'Aziz b. Yahya al-Juludi a Book of the Poetry of 'Ali, peace be upon him.

As for the Book of al-Shihab, although it is among the compositions of those who differ from us, most of its clauses are set down in the books and reports transmitted by our paths; for that reason our scholars relied upon it and undertook to comment upon it. Al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din said: "Al-Sayyid Fakhr al-Din Shumayla b. Muhammad b. Abi Hashim al-Husayni, a righteous scholar; he transmitted to us the Book of al-Shihab of the judge Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad b. Salama b. Ja'far al-Quda'i, from him."
Al-Shaykh Abu al-Futuh is well known for learning, and his books are recognised and familiar.
The Book of al-Anwar al-Badriyya contains some evident benefits.

The History of the City of Qum is a reliable book, but the original of the book was not available to us; only its translation reached us, and we have extracted some of its reports in the Book of the Heavens and the World.
The answers to the questions of Ibn Salam we have set down in their places.

As for the Book of Tibb al-Nabi, may God bless him and his family, although most of its reports are by the paths of those who differ from us, it is well known and in circulation among our scholars. Nasir al-Milla wa'l-Din al-Tusi said in the Book of Adab al-Muta'allimin: "He must learn something of medicine and seek blessing in the traditions handed down on medicine which the Shaykh and Imam Abu al-'Abbas al-Mustaghfiri gathered in his book entitled Tibb al-Nabi, may God bless him and his family."

Al-Muhaqqiq al-Ardabili reached the utmost limit in scrupulousness, godfearing, asceticism and learning; I have not heard of his like among the earlier or the later scholars. May God join him with the pure Imams. His books are of the utmost exactitude and investigation.

Al-Khalil and al-Sahib were both of the Imamiyya, and both are landmarks in lexicography, prosody and Arabic. Al-Sahib is he in whose name al-Saduq prefaced 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, peace be upon him, and to whom he presented it.
Al-Shawahid is a good book containing an exposition of the revelation of the verses concerning the People of the House, peace be upon them,

43.text: and al-Tabrisi and other leading scholars often cite from it.
Al-Maqsad contains rare reports and unusual rulings, some of which we set down for corroboration and confirmation.
Al-'Umda is the best known and most reliable of books on genealogy.

Al-Narsi is among the possessors of primary works; he transmitted from al-Sadiq and al-Kazim, peace be upon them both. Al-Najashi set down his chain to Ibn Abi 'Umayr from him; al-Shaykh in al-Tahdhib and elsewhere transmits from his book; and al-Kulayni likewise transmitted from his book in several places — among them, in the chapter on kissing, from 'Ali b. Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from him; and among them, in the Book of Fasting, by another chain from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from him.

So too the book of Zayd al-Zarrad, from which the people of learning and right guidance have drawn. Al-Najashi likewise set down his chain to Ibn Abi 'Umayr from him. Al-Shaykh said in the Fihrist and the Rijal: "They have two primary works which Ibn Babawayh and Ibn al-Walid did not transmit; Ibn al-Walid used to say that the two are forged." And Ibn al-Ghada'iri said: "Abu Ja'far erred in this statement, for I have seen their books heard from Muhammad b. Abi 'Umayr." End of quotation. I say: although the masters of rijal did not attest their trustworthiness, the fact that the greatest of the traditionists drew from their two books and relied upon them — even al-Saduq in Ma'ani al-Akhbar and elsewhere — together with Ibn Abi 'Umayr's transmission from them and al-Shaykh's counting their book among the primary works, is perhaps enough to permit reliance upon them. Besides which, we took them from an old, corrected copy in the hand of al-Shaykh Mansur b. al-Hasan al-Abi, who transmitted it from the hand of the eminent Shaykh Muhammad b. al-Hasan al-Qummi; the date of its writing was the year three hundred and seventy-four. He mentioned that he took these and the rest of the primary works mentioned hereafter from the hand of the most eminent Shaykh Harun b. Musa al-Tal'ukbari, God have mercy on him. At the beginning of al-Narsi's book he set down his chain thus: "There narrated to us the Shaykh Abu Muhammad Harun b. Musa al-Tal'ukbari, may God support him, who said: There narrated to us Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad b. Muhammad b. Sa'id al-Hamadani, who said: There narrated to us Ja'far b. 'Abd Allah al-'Alawi Abu 'Abd Allah al-Muhammadi, who said: There narrated to us Muhammad b. Abi 'Umayr, from Zayd al-Narsi." And at the beginning of al-Zarrad's book he set down his chain thus: "There narrated to us Abu Muhammad Harun b. Musa al-Tal'ukbari, from Abu 'Ali Muhammad b. Hammam, from Humayd b. Ziyad b. Hammad, from Abu al-'Abbas 'Ubayd Allah b. Ahmad b.

44.text: Nuhayk, from Muhammad b. Abi 'Umayr, from Zayd al-Zarrad." These two chains differ from what al-Najashi set down.

The book of al-'Usfuri we likewise took from the aforementioned copy. The chain is set down at its beginning thus: "There informed us al-Tal'ukbari, from Muhammad b. Hammam, from Muhammad b. Ahmad b. Khaqan al-Nahdi, from Abu Samina, from Abu Sa'id al-'Usfuri, 'Abbad." Al-Shaykh and al-Najashi, God have mercy on them both, mentioned his book and set down their chain to him, but did not attest his trustworthiness; perhaps his reports are fit to serve for corroboration.
The book of 'Asim — its author is recognised for trustworthiness and eminence.

Al-Shaykh and al-Najashi set down chains to his book. In the aforementioned copy his chain runs thus: "There narrated to me Abu al-Hasan Muhammad b. al-Hasan b. al-Husayn b. Ayyub al-Qummi, may God support him, who said: There narrated to me Abu Muhammad Harun b. Musa al-Tal'ukbari, from Abu 'Ali Muhammad b. Hammam b. Suhayl the scribe, from Humayd b. Ziyad b. Hawara in the year three hundred and nine, from 'Abd Allah b. Ahmad b. Nuhayk, from Musawir and Salama, from 'Asim b. Humayd al-Hannat." Al-Tal'ukbari said: "There also narrated to me this book Abu al-Qasim Ja'far b. Muhammad b. Ibrahim al-'Alawi al-Musawi, at Cairo, from Ibn Nuhayk."

As for the book of Ibn al-Hadrami, al-Shaykh set down his route to it in the Fihrist; and in the aforementioned copy his chain is set down thus: "There informed us the Shaykh Abu Muhammad Harun b. Musa al-Tal'ukbari, may God support him, from Muhammad b. Hammam, from Humayd b. Ziyad al-Dihqan, from Abu Ja'far Ahmad b. Zayd b. Ja'far al-Asadi al-Bazzaz, from Muhammad b. al-Muthanna b. al-Qasim al-Hadrami, from Ja'far b. Muhammad b. Shurayh al-Hadrami." Al-Shaykh likewise transmitted from a company, from al-Tal'ukbari, to the end of the foregoing chain, except that his has "from Muhammad b. Umayya b. al-Qasim"; and it appears that what is here is the more correct. Most of its reports terminate with Jabir al-Ju'fi.

As for the book of Muhammad b. al-Muthanna b. al-Qasim al-Hadrami, al-Najashi attested its author's trustworthiness and set down his route to it. In the aforementioned old copy his chain is given thus: "There narrated to us the Shaykh Harun b. Musa al-Tal'ukbari, from Muhammad b. Hammam, from Humayd b. Ziyad, from Ahmad b. Zayd b. Ja'far al-Azdi al-Bazzaz, from Muhammad b. al-Muthanna."

45.text: As for the book of 'Abd al-Malik b. Hakim, al-Najashi attested the author's trustworthiness, and both he and al-Shaykh set down their route to it. In the old copy his route runs thus: "There informed us al-Tal'ukbari, from Ibn 'Uqda, from 'Ali b. al-Hasan b. Faddal, from Ja'far b. Muhammad b. Hakim, from his uncle 'Abd al-Malik."

As for the book of al-Muthanna, al-Shaykh and al-Najashi set down their route to it, and al-Kashshi transmitted from 'Ali b. al-Hasan his praise. In the aforementioned copy his chain runs thus: "Al-Tal'ukbari, from Ibn 'Uqda, from 'Ali b. al-Hasan b. Faddal, from al-'Abbas b. 'Amir, from Muthanna b. al-Walid al-Hannat."

As for the book of Khallad, al-Najashi and al-Shaykh set down their chain to it. In the old copy it runs thus: "Al-Tal'ukbari, from Ibn 'Uqda, from Yahya b. Zakariyya b. Shayban, from Muhammad b. Abi 'Umayr, from Khallad al-Sindi" — and in some copies al-Suddi, without the nun — "al-Bazzaz al-Kufi."

As for the book of al-Husayn b. 'Uthman, al-Najashi set down a chain to it, and al-Kashshi and others attested his trustworthiness. The chain in the old copy we have runs: "From al-Tal'ukbari, from Ibn 'Uqda, from Ja'far b. 'Abd Allah al-Muhammadi, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from al-Husayn b. 'Uthman b. Sharik."

As for the book of al-Kahili, its author is praised, and al-Shaykh and al-Najashi gave chains from him. The chain in the old copy runs: "From al-Tal'ukbari, from Ibn 'Uqda, from Muhammad b. Ahmad b. al-Hasan b. al-Hakam al-Qatawani, from Ahmad b. Muhammad b. Abi Nasr, from 'Abd Allah b. Yahya."

As for the book of Sallam b. 'Amra al-Khurasani, al-Najashi attested his trustworthiness and gave a chain to the book. In our copy: "Al-Tal'ukbari, from Ibn 'Uqda, from al-Qasim b. Muhammad b. al-Hasan (1) b. Hazim, from 'Abd Allah b. Jamila, from Sallam."

As for the Book of al-Nawadir, its author is trustworthy though a Fathi; al-Najashi and al-Shaykh gave chains from him. The chain in our copy runs: "From al-Tal'ukbari, from Ibn 'Uqda, from 'Ali b. al-Hasan b. Faddal, from Ibn Asbat."
As for the Book of al-Nabdha, we do not know the condition of its author.
Al-Duristi is among the students of al-Mufid and al-Murtada; Ibn Dawud, al-'Allama, al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din and others attested his trustworthiness.

46.text: The Book of al-Karr wa'l-Farr is well known and contains noble answers.

The Book of al-Arba'in is among the recognised books. Al-Shaykh Ibrahim al-Qatifi, God have mercy on him, was of the utmost learning; he was a contemporary of al-Shaykh Nur al-Din the promoter, and between them were many disputations and debates.

Then know that we shall set down some of the reports of the foregoing books from which we have not taken much, for certain reasons, together with such books as newly appear, in a separate book which we have named Mustadrak al-Bihar, if God the Generous and Forgiving wills — since appending them to this book would occasion the alteration of many copies already dispersed through the lands. God is the granter of success in what is good, right and sound.
Chapter Three: The sigla assigned to those books

We set them at the head of every report so that it may be known from which primary work it is taken, and whether it is in a single work or repeated across the works. Where there is a difference in the chain, we set the report down from one of the two books and refer to the other after it, carrying it through to the point of agreement. Where there is a difference in the text that alters the meaning, we make it clear. Where the content is the same but the wording differs and the report suits two chapters, we set it down with one wording in the one chapter and with the other wording in the other.

Let us then set down the sigla: n for 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, peace be upon him; ' for 'Ilal al-Shara'i'; k for Ikmal al-Din; yd for al-Tawhid; l for al-Khisal; li for the Amali of al-Saduq; thw for Thawab al-A'mal; m' for Ma'ani al-Akhbar; hd for al-Hidaya; 'd for al-'Aqa'id. As for the rest of al-Saduq's books and the two books of his father, we had no need of sigla for them, their reports being few. b for Qurb al-Isnad; yr for Basa'ir al-Darajat; ma for the Amali of al-Shaykh; ght for the Ghayba of al-Shaykh; msba for the two Misbahs; sha for al-Irshad; ja for the Majalis of al-Mufid; khts for the Book of al-Ikhtisas. For the rest of the books of al-Mufid and

47.text: al-Shaykh we have assigned no siglum; likewise for the Amali of al-Shaykh's son, which we have joined with his father's Amali under one siglum, since he transmits all its reports from his father, God be pleased with them both.

ml for Kamil al-Ziyara; sn for al-Mahasin; fs for the commentary of 'Ali b. Ibrahim; shy for the commentary of al-'Ayyashi; m for the commentary of the Imam, peace be upon him; dh for Rawdat al-Wa'izin; 'm for I'lam al-Wara; mka for Makarim al-Akhlaq; j for al-Ihtijaj; qb for the Manaqib of Ibn Shahrashub; kshf for Kashf al-Ghumma; f for Tuhaf al-'Uqul; md for al-'Umda; ns for al-Kifaya; nbh for Tanbih al-Khatir; nhj for Nahj al-Balagha; tb for Tibb al-A'imma; sh for Sahifat al-Rida, peace be upon him; da for Fiqh al-Rida, peace be upon him; yj for al-Khara'ij; s for Qisas al-Anbiya'; daw' for Daw' al-Shihab; ta for Aman al-Akhtar; shf for Kashf al-Yaqin.

yf for al-Tara'if; qih for al-Duru'; fth for Fath al-Abwab; njm for the Book of al-Nujum; jm for Jamal al-Usbu'; ql for Iqbal al-A'mal; tm for Falah al-Sa'il, it being among the completions of al-Misbah; mhj for Muhaj al-Da'awat; sba for Misbah al-Za'ir; ha for Farhat al-Ghari; knz for Kanz Jami' al-Fawa'id and Ta'wil al-Ayat al-Zahira together, since one of them is taken from the other, as you have learned; ghw for Ghawali al-La'ali — and al-Nathr needs no siglum; j' for Jami' al-Akhbar; ni for the Ghayba of al-Nu'mani; fd for the Book of al-Rawda, it being on the merits; ms for Misbah al-Shari'a; qbs for Qabas al-Misbah; t for al-Sirat al-Mustaqim; khs for Muntakhab al-Basa'ir; sr for al-Sara'ir; q for the ancient Ghurawi book; ksh for the Rijal of al-Kashshi; jsh for the Fihrist of al-Najashi; bsha for Bisharat al-Mustafa; yn for the two books of al-Husayn b. Sa'id, or for his book and al-Nawadir; 'yn for al-'Uyun wa'l-Mahasin; ghr for al-Ghurar wa'l-Durar; kf for the Misbah of al-Kaf'ami; ld for al-Balad al-Amin; qda for Qada' al-Huquq; mhs for al-Tamhis; 'dh for al-'Udda; jnh for al-Junna; mnha for al-Minhaj; d for al-'Adad; yl for al-Fada'il; fr for the commentary of Furat b. Ibrahim; 'a for Da'a'im al-Islam.

The remaining books have no siglum; we simply give their names in full. Among them are those we have set down in full in the places suited to them, such as Tibb al-Rida, peace be upon him, the Tawhid of al-Mufaddal, al-Ihlilaja, and

48.text: the Book of al-Masa'il of 'Ali b. Ja'far, and the Fihrist of al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din. We assigned them no siglum either because they are set down in full in their places, as you have learned; or because our recourse to them is slight, most of their reports being from the wider community; or because the book is of small bulk and its reports few; or because of the absence of complete reliance upon it; or for other such considerations and purposes.

Then know that we have left aside setting down the reports of certain widely transmitted books in this book of ours — such as the four books — because they are widely transmitted and carefully preserved, so that perhaps it is not permissible to expend effort in copying them and leaving them aside. Yet if in some places we need to set down a report from them, these are their sigla: ka for al-Kafi; yb for al-Tahdhib; sa for al-Istibsar; yh for Man la Yahduruhu al-Faqih. When we come to the derivative rulings we shall leave the sigla aside and give the names explicitly, if God the Exalted wills, for benefits particular to that which are not hidden from men of understanding. And there too we shall leave aside the abbreviations in the chains which we have adopted in the following section, given how much the chain is needed there.
Chapter Four: Conventions adopted for abbreviating the chains of transmission

— while guarding against the omission that leads to slight reliance. For most compilers have made a habit of lengthening their mention of the men of a report, so as to adorn the book and multiply the chapters; while some of them drop the chains altogether, so that the reports thereby fall from the rank of those with full chains, and the distinction between reports in strength and weakness, completeness and deficiency, is lost — for it is by the reporter that the standing of the report is known, and it is by reliance upon the transmitters that the loftiness of a narration and a tradition is inferred. So we chose to set down the chain in its entirety while observing the utmost concision: contenting ourselves, in the case of well-known men, with mentioning their father, or their title, or their bare name, without ascription to grandfather or father and without mention of the descriptive epithet, the agnomen and the title; and, where a chain recurs often across the chapters, referring to the whole of it by a siglum, a mark and a convention laid down at the head of the book — so that nothing of the benefits of the primary works should be left out of our book and it thereby fall from the rank of complete acceptability.
